paragraphs: The Dutch Shepherd was shaped as a herding dog that also took on police and protection work, and the modern dog still wants a job in the handler's hands. Adults land between 42 and 75 pounds and 21.5 to 24.5 inches, with a reliable, alert, trainable temperament and excellent trainability. Exercise on this card is very high, two hours and more, because the work drive does not burn off on a single evening stroll. Children fit well after real socialization, while other dogs are only a moderate match. Shedding runs moderate to high and changes with the short, long, or rough coat.

Plan the house around a dog that stays watchful. A Dutch Shepherd bonds hard to one handler and notices the street, the hallway, and the delivery at the door, so a yard without a training plan just produces a bored guardian of the sofa. Give the two-plus hours as herding-style games, tracking, or obedience with a clear release, not as endless ball throwing that winds the drive higher. Other dogs in the home need introductions on purpose, because the breed card rates that fit as moderate. Puppies that learn a settle cue are easier to live with once the adult weight, anywhere from 42 to 75 pounds, arrives.

Feed for the work, and watch the skin. Premium food for a Dutch Shepherd is listed at $600 to $1,200 a year, which has to cover a medium-to-large dog doing very high exercise. Some lines develop skin allergies, so a sudden itch, ear redness, or a coat that looks dusty is a reason to talk with the vet before you rotate bags for fun. Hip and elbow dysplasia show up in active dogs, so keep the body lean while those joints are still building. Goniodysplasia can disturb fluid drainage in the eye and lead to glaucoma, and progressive retinal atrophy has a genetic test worth asking a breeder to show. Inflammatory myopathy, a muscle inflammation reported in the breed, is another reason not to ignore a dog that suddenly tires or seems stiff after ordinary work.

Before an East European Shepherd puppy comes home, ask what was checked on the parents. This heavy working shepherd runs 75 to 130 pounds and 24 to 30 inches, and the card flags hip dysplasia as possible though less widespread than in German Shepherds, plus elbow dysplasia. Breeding dogs should have cardiac screening. Eyes deserve regular exams. Bloat, the stomach emergency called GDV, is a risk in this deep chest, and some veterinarians discuss a preventive gastropexy. A DNA panel does not replace those orthopedic and heart records, but it belongs in the same folder as the OFA paperwork.

An East European Shepherd often reaches the later years somewhere inside a 10 to 14 year span, and the change shows up as a slower rise from the bed rather than a sudden collapse of the working mind. Shorten the 1 to 2 hour outing before the dog asks you to, and keep the double coat brushed so mats do not hide a new lump or a thin spot. Sensitive stomachs in some lines mean a senior food switch should be gradual. Heart checks that were wise for breeding stock are still wise when the dog is older and the exercise day gets quieter.

Routine veterinary care for an East European Shepherd is listed at $350 to $700 a year, with insurance often $500 to $950. Use those visits for hips, elbows, eyes, and a hands-on check of a dog this large, not only for vaccines. Owners who wait until a 75 to 130 pound dog is already lame pay for a crisis on top of the ordinary bill. The temperament is described as loyal, protective, and balanced when the dog is well bred, so a sudden irritability can be pain rather than a personality change.

A big double-coated shepherd with a sometimes touchy stomach does not need a new diet trend every season. Premium food runs $800 to $1,500 a year at this size. Split meals and skip hard running right after eating, because bloat is the emergency you are trying not to meet. If a dog in the line has had digestive sensitivities, keep the protein source steady once stools are firm, and treat itching from skin allergies as a medical question. The 1 to 2 hours of daily work still require calories, so measure the cup against the ribs rather than against the picture on the bag.

On an East European Shepherd food bag, read the life-stage statement and the calorie count per cup before you admire the front photo. A 24 to 30 inch dog can gain weight quietly under a heavy coat. Protein and fat have to support high exercise without turning every meal into a rich feast that bothers a sensitive stomach. Grooming costs of $150 to $350 a year are mostly about that coat, not about a salon haircut, and a dog that is itchy from allergies may need the vet more than a different label design.

Living with an East European Shepherd is a long partnership with a loyal, protective dog that can be dominant around other dogs and reserved with strangers. Experienced handlers get the excellent trainability the card describes. First-year training is listed at $500 to $1,500 because manners on a 75 to 130 pound dog are not optional. The dog should settle in the house after 1 to 2 hours of real work, watch the family without inventing threats, and keep that balanced temperament the breed notes praise.

The English Bulldog left the old bull-baiting ring and became a short, heavy companion of about 40 to 50 pounds and 14 to 15 inches. The temperament on this card is calm, courageous, and friendly, and the fit with children is excellent. Exercise stays low: about 30 to 45 minutes of gentle walking and light play, not a jogging program. Lifespan is listed at 8 to 10 years, which is the number to read before the wrinkles win you over. Shedding and grooming needs are both low, though the folds still need a daily look.

Middle age arrives early on an 8 to 10 year clock. An English Bulldog that used to finish a 30 to 45 minute amble and now stops to breathe at the curb needs the walk shortened and the heat respected. The flat face and thick body do not cool the way a longer-muzzled dog does, so summer outings move to the cool part of the day. Courageous does not mean athletic. Friendly and calm is the household the breed actually suits, with excellent manners around children who are not allowed to pile onto a dog that is already down.

Premium food for an English Bulldog is listed at $400 to $800 a year, and the useful test is a lean waist on a 40 to 50 pound frame, not a fancy ingredient panel. Extra fat makes the already low exercise day harder and shortens a life listed at only 8 to 10 years. Feed measured meals, keep treats inside that budget, and skip the idea that a calm dog can free-feed. Routine veterinary care runs $300 to $600 and insurance $300 to $600, which is where breathing, skin folds, and weight belong on the agenda. Grooming is a modest $100 to $300 because the coat is short, while the folds and the tail pocket still need cleaning at home.

English Cocker Spaniels were bred to flush and retrieve in dense cover, and the house dog still carries that merry, busy spaniel motor. Adults weigh about 26 to 34 pounds and stand 15 to 17 inches, with a moderate shed and a high grooming need on the feathered ears and legs. Exercise is high. Children are an excellent match. A lifespan of 12 to 14 years is realistic when the ears stay dry and the dog gets work instead of only a lap.

A great home for an English Cocker Spaniel treats the merry temperament as a working brain with the day off, not as a decorative spaniel. The dog is affectionate and busy, so a quiet house all week and a huge Saturday hike leaves a 26 to 34 pound athlete inventing jobs in the laundry. High exercise belongs on the weekday calendar. The long coat that makes grooming a $300 to $600 line item also hides mats behind the ears if nobody handles feet and feathering while the dog is young.

Health for an English Cocker Spaniel is mostly repetition. Keep the pendulous ears clean and dry after fieldwork or a bath, because that heavy leather traps moisture. Keep the body light enough for high daily exercise across a 12 to 14 year life. Routine veterinary care is listed at $300 to $600 a year. Watch the merry mood: a busy spaniel that suddenly opts out of a walk is telling you something a vaccine visit alone will not catch. Insurance on this card runs $300 to $600.

The quick-facts table puts premium food at $400 to $800, routine veterinary care at $300 to $600, insurance at $300 to $600, grooming at $300 to $600, first-year training at $200 to $500, and supplies at $150 to $300. Those grooming and food lines move with how often the feathering is professionally done and how hard the dog works. A city clinic and a rural one will not bill the same $300 to $600 veterinary band. The dog's own ears, weight, and activity change the year more than the average does.

The first year with an English Cocker Spaniel stacks puppy visits, the $200 to $500 training line, a crate, and the start of a grooming habit that later sits at $300 to $600 a year. After that, the annual picture is food at $400 to $800 plus routine care, insurance, and supplies at $150 to $300. As the dog moves through the 12 to 14 year span, ear care and a slower body can push veterinary spending up even when the purchase price is long forgotten.

Put the English Cocker Spaniel on a calendar: ears, nails, teeth, and a yearly exam inside the $300 to $600 routine veterinary band, with insurance listed at $300 to $600 if you want help when a spaniel problem stops being routine. High exercise only stays healthy if the dog is lean. The merry, affectionate nature makes them easy to overfeed from the hand. Grooming at $300 to $600 is part of health here, because matted feathering and a wet ear are how small spaniel issues become painful ones.

Over a 12 to 14 year life, the English Cocker Spaniel's coat, weight, and energy show whether the bowl matches a high-exercise sporting dog of 26 to 34 pounds. Premium food is listed at $400 to $800. A dull feathered coat or a spaniel that is busy at dinner and flat on the walk is a reason to review portions with the clinic, not to keep adding toppers. Moderate shedding does not mean the coat can be ignored between the $300 to $600 grooming visits.

Choose an English Cocker Spaniel food by the dog in front of you: 15 to 17 inches, high daily exercise, and a feathered coat that still has to be brushed at home. Look for a complete diet suited to that life, then measure it. Supplies and toys at $150 to $300 can include chew items, but they should not become a second dinner for an affectionate dog that follows you into the kitchen. If stools or ears worsen after a bag change, go back to the last food that kept this spaniel merry and comfortable.

English Setters were developed to range, point, and keep a gentle partnership with a hunter on foot. The companion still stands 23 to 27 inches and weighs 45 to 80 pounds, with a moderate shed and a high need for both exercise and grooming. Temperament is gentle, mellow, and merry, and the rating with children is excellent. The lifespan line on this card is 12 years, so the feathered coat and the running gear have to be looked after for a long sporting life.

Read an English Setter by the job, not by the soft expression alone. Gentle and mellow in the house still comes with high exercise and a merry streak that wants birds, fields, or a long sniffling outing. The silky feathering that drives grooming to $300 to $600 a year mats if it is only bathed. At 45 to 80 pounds they are large enough to bowl over a child who was promised a couch dog, even though the breed is excellent with kids who understand a happy setter greeting. Trainability is real, and so is the need to tire the dog before you ask for stillness.

The middle of an English Toy Spaniel's 10 to 12 year life is when the heart and the flat face ask for a quieter day. Mitral valve disease, a progressive valve problem the breed notes call very common, can show up as a cough, faster tiring, or less interest in the 20 to 30 minutes of easy exercise this 8 to 14 pound dog is supposed to enjoy. Patent ductus arteriosus, a congenital heart defect seen occasionally, is a puppy question for the vet. Keep play short, keep rooms cool, and do not treat a slower toy spaniel as lazy.

Money for an English Toy Spaniel is not mostly food. Premium food is $200 to $400 a year, while routine veterinary care is $300 to $600, insurance $350 to $650, and grooming $300 to $500 because the coat and the heavy ears need help. First-year training sits at $150 to $350 and supplies at $100 to $200. A dog with very common mitral valve disease, patellar luxation, or eye trouble such as cherry eye, cataracts, or retinal disease can leave those ranges. Heat illness from the shortened airway is the expensive day you avoid by staying indoors when the weather turns.

An English Toy Spaniel of 8 to 14 pounds and 10 to 11 inches needs a steady, modest bowl, not a rotating menu. Exercise is low, about 20 to 30 minutes, so calories pile up fast on a brachycephalic dog that already works harder to breathe. Brachycephalic syndrome and heat sensitivity are husbandry facts here: feed and walk in the cool, and stop if the dog struggles. Long, heavy ears trap moisture and lead to ear infections, so drying ears is part of the feeding-day routine, not a separate hobby. Grooming at $300 to $500 a year keeps the coat out of those ears.

Match the English Toy Spaniel's food to a gentle, playful, affectionate toy that prefers a peaceful room and may be shy with strangers at first. The nutritional job is maintaining a lean 8 to 14 pound body that can do 20 to 30 minutes of easy play without respiratory strain. Patellar luxation, common in toy dogs, gets worse with extra weight. Eye problems, including cherry eye, cataracts, and retinal issues, are not fixed by a grain-free slogan. Read the calorie line, measure the cup, and spend the veterinary budget of $300 to $600 on hearts, knees, eyes, and ears rather than on boutique toppers.

An Entlebucher Mountain Dog is the smallest of the Swiss mountain dogs and a herder, not a pasture guardian and not a sprinter. Social life starts with that herding mouth. The breed notes warn that herding instinct may nip at the heels of children or other pets, so puppy greetings need a toy and a cutoff word, not a lecture after the fact. Adults are 40 to 65 pounds and 16 to 21 inches, loyal, confident, and energetic, and they can be protective, which makes early socialization essential. Other dogs and children are rated good when that work is actually done. Beginner-friendly sits at 3 out of 5 because this is a herding-dog home, not a casual one.

Through the middle of an 11 to 13 year Entlebucher life, watch urine, eyes, and the way the dog rises. Ectopic ureter is a breed condition to screen for, especially in females, and a young female that leaks is not a dog that simply needs another antibiotic. Progressive retinal atrophy, including prcd-PRA, and cataracts are reasons for eye exams as the dog leaves early adulthood. Hemolytic anemia is on the breed list, so unexplained weakness or pale gums belongs with a veterinarian. High exercise is still required, but a herder that skips a stride may be a knee, a back, or a systemic problem rather than a training slump.

Feed an Entlebucher Mountain Dog like a 40 to 65 pound herding dog with high daily work, and keep the bowl boring once it agrees with the dog. Premium food is listed at $400 to $900. There is no glory in rotating proteins for a breed whose serious problems are ectopic ureters, eyes, and hemolytic anemia rather than a mysterious need for a new kibble every month. Measure portions so the tricolor coat stays on a lean body. Supplies at $150 to $350 should include legal chew items, because a confident, energetic herder will pick the baseboard if you do not.

The guaranteed analysis and the calorie statement matter more than the Swiss-chalet photo on an Entlebucher bag. A 16 to 21 inch dog with high exercise and high trainability burns food, then gains quietly if the cup creeps up. Protein and fat should fit that work. Grooming is a wide $100 to $400 because the coat is short and shedding is only moderate, so most of the care budget is not a salon. If you change food, change it because stools, weight, or itch changed, and give the new bag time before you declare it a cure.

First-year Entlebucher costs hide in the herding brain. Food may fall in the $400 to $900 band and routine veterinary care in the $300 to $600 band, with insurance at $350 to $700, but the surprise is often a chewed crate, a second fence line, or a class you add because a 3-out-of-5 beginner dog is nipping heels. Supplies start at $150 to $350 and climb if you replace what the energetic youngster destroys. Ask the breeder about ectopic ureter screening in females and prcd-PRA before you add those bills to a dog you could have skipped.

Preventive care for an Entlebucher Mountain Dog means eyes, urinary continence in young females, and a body condition you can feel under a moderate coat. The breed list includes progressive retinal atrophy, cataracts, ectopic ureter, and hemolytic anemia. A leaking female puppy needs a workup, not a repeating antibiotic and a shrug. Routine care is priced at $300 to $600 a year on this card. Insurance at $350 to $700 is the line that matters if an eye or a urinary problem leaves the ordinary visit. High trainability makes husbandry easier if you start it before the dog has a hobby of herding the children.

Socialize an Entlebucher Mountain Dog while the herding and guarding instincts are still flexible. The classic sensitive window runs from about 3 to 14 weeks, and this breed needs people, children, livestock sounds, and other dogs in that stretch, with the mouth on a toy instead of on ankles. The card says good with kids and good with other dogs, and also that the dog can be protective and may nip heels. Both are true. A puppy that meets the world on a loose lead becomes the loyal, confident adult. A puppy that rehearses herding the toddler does not grow out of it by charm.

A puppy class is the right next step after home socialization for an Entlebucher, because high trainability still needs a plan. Use the class to proof sit, a settle, and a leave-it around motion, which is the moment a herder wants to nip. Keep going after the six-week course: markets, quiet stock at a distance, new floors, friendly dogs. Grooming practice belongs there too, even though professional grooming may only be $100 to $400. The goal is a 40 to 65 pound dog that can be handled for eyes, urine checks, and nails without a fight.

Daily life with an Entlebucher Mountain Dog goes better on a clock. High exercise and a confident, energetic temperament mean a morning outing, a training fragment, and an evening outing, then a real off switch. Do not let the dog practice herding children as the evening hobby. Feed from the $400 to $900 food budget on a schedule so you notice a skipped meal. A young female that suddenly drinks more or leaks on the bed needs a vet visit aimed at ectopic ureter, not a longer walk. Every dog varies, but this breed varies inside herding work, not inside a no-training household.

An Estrela Mountain Dog is a livestock guardian from the mountains of Portugal, large to giant at 77 to 132 pounds and 24.5 to 29 inches, and it is not a sighthound that should be asked to course game. The useful owner learns the independent guardian mind: loyal and devoted, protective and territorial, intelligent enough to sort a real threat from a normal afternoon, and gentler with family children than the size suggests. Trainability is moderate because the dog was bred to decide. Exercise is a moderate 1 to 1.5 hours, including time to patrol, not a sprint session.

Social manners in an Estrela Mountain Dog are built early and then maintained, because a territorial guardian does not become casual on its own. Puppies that meet guests, children, and other dogs while the handler is clearly in charge grow into the excellent-with-family rating. Other dogs are only a moderate fit and can be dominant. Strangers should be introduced, not surprised at the gate. Two coat varieties both shed heavily, so handling for grooming starts in puppyhood. The adult that has patrolled a yard for years still needs refreshers, or the protective instinct writes its own rules.

Screen an Estrela Mountain Dog for the problems the breed actually lists. Hips and elbows can be dysplastic in a dog of this weight, so OFA-style evaluations on the parents matter. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the heart condition to watch, which means a cardiac exam belongs in the file. Eyes can show entropion or progressive retinal atrophy. Bloat, GDV, is a risk in large deep-chested dogs, and a preventive plan with your veterinarian is part of owning 77 to 132 pounds of guardian. None of that is a sighthound panel. It is orthopedic, cardiac, eye, and stomach care for a flock guardian.

The first year with an Estrela Mountain Dog fronts the $400 to $1,200 training line, because an independent guardian does not train itself, plus a fence that actually holds a dog whose job is territory. Food for a large-to-giant body is $700 to $1,400, routine veterinary care $350 to $700, and supplies $250 to $500 before you replace what a youngster chews. Later years still carry insurance at $500 to $900 and grooming at $200 to $400 for one of the two heavy coats. Spending eases only after the adult manners exist. It rises again if bloat, hips, or a heart problem shows up inside the 10 to 14 year span.

A yearly plan for an Estrela Mountain Dog puts weight, heart, eyes, and the stomach on the calendar. Routine care is $350 to $700. Insurance is often $500 to $900, which is worth understanding before a GDV surgery or a dilated cardiomyopathy workup. Keep the dog lean under whichever coat variety you have. High shedding is not a health plan. Walk the moderate 1 to 1.5 hours and allow patrol time so the guardian instinct has a legal outlet. Entropion that makes a dog squint is a veterinary problem, not a personality called protective.

What an Estrela Mountain Dog eats has to hold a 77 to 132 pound guardian at a working lean, with enough fuel for 1 to 1.5 hours of moderate patrol and not so much bulk that hips, elbows, and bloat risk get worse. Premium food is listed at $700 to $1,400. There is no single recipe. Watch stools, the waist, and energy on territory walks. A dog that is dull, pot-bellied, or suddenly restless after meals needs the bowl and the vet reviewed. Coat condition on either of the two varieties tells you whether the diet is keeping up with heavy shedding.

Ignore the mountain photography on an Estrela food bag and read whether the diet is complete for a large adult, what the calories per cup are, and whether the dog stays lean on the measured amount. Balanced protein and fat matter for a guardian that patrols rather than sprints. If you are feeding for a made-up racing dog, you have the wrong breed. This is a livestock guardian with moderate exercise. Grooming at $200 to $400 maintains the coat the food is supposed to support. It does not fix a skinny dog or an overweight one.

People who have actually kept an Estrela Mountain Dog describe the early months as the negotiation, and the later years as the point. Once the independent thinker trusts the household, the loyal, gentle-with-family side is obvious, including with children. The dog remains reserved and territorial, needs space to watch, and will not turn into an off-leash coursing hound. Budget grooming, the $500 to $900 insurance band, and a veterinarian who knows bloat and large-breed hearts. By the time the dog is mature, 1 to 1.5 hours and a job at the edge of the property feel ordinary.

A Field Spaniel stays healthier when the handler stays gentle and repetitive. This is a docile, sensitive sporting dog of 35 to 50 pounds and 17 to 18 inches, and harsh corrections can shut the dog down. The serious list is hips, patellar luxation, progressive retinal atrophy with a DNA test available, cataracts in some lines, ectropion or entropion, ear infections under the long pendulous leather, and hypothyroidism. Excellent with respectful children and very good with other dogs does not replace ear drying, eye checks, and a lean body across 12 to 13 years. Routine care is listed at $300 to $600 a year.

A Field Spaniel fits a household that wants the dog in the room. They are devoted, fun-loving under a calm surface, and reserved with strangers until they feel safe, and they can suffer if left alone too long. Exercise is moderate to high, an hour and up, of outing and training rather than a harsh drill. Grooming runs $300 to $600 because of the spaniel coat. First-year training at $200 to $800 should be positive, matching a dog the card calls sensitive to correction. Food at $500 to $900 and insurance at $400 to $700 sit beside that, for a 12 to 13 year companion everyone actually lives with.

Caring for a Finnish Lapphund means remembering a reindeer herder, not a livestock guardian left alone with a flock and not a sighthound. Adults are 33 to 53 pounds and 16 to 21 inches, friendly, alert, and agile, excellent with children, with moderate shedding and a high grooming need. Exercise is moderate, and the activities that suit them are herding trials, agility, obedience, and rally. Epilepsy is a condition owners should discuss with a veterinarian. MDR1 drug sensitivity is a breed concern breeders should screen for, and the result belongs in the clinic file before anesthesia or a new prescription. Lifespan is 12 to 15 years.

Make physical room for a double coat and mental room for a herding dog. A Finnish Lapphund will shed through the house on a moderate cycle and will need the $300 to $600 grooming line, or a serious home brushing habit, if you want the pants and the tail to survive. Premium food is $400 to $800. The dog is agile and friendly, so stairs full of children are fine only when the herding mouth has been taught not to run the household. Insurance at $300 to $600 and routine care at $300 to $600 should include the epilepsy conversation and the MDR1 status, not only vaccines. Supplies at $150 to $300 cover brushes you will actually use.

A Finnish Spitz is a barking bird dog from Finland, friendly, alert, and playful, and the care that matters is noise, fence, and the parents' health notes. Adults weigh 20 to 33 pounds and stand 15 to 20 inches, with heavy shedding and moderate-to-high exercise. Trainability is moderate. Beginner-friendly is 3 out of 5. Patellar luxation and hypothyroidism are conditions to know. The breed notes also tell a buyer to ask what the parents' line did about epilepsy and hips. This is not a quiet white companion spitz, and it is not a flock guardian.

Housing a Finnish Spitz starts with a house that can absorb the voice. The breed is extremely vocal, and a noise-restricted apartment is the wrong building. They may be aloof with strangers at first, then friendly, and they are excellent with children and good with other dogs. Heavy shedding means a coat plan, with grooming listed anywhere from $100 to $400. Prey drive is strong enough that squirrels can erase a recall, so the yard needs a real fence. Off-leash hiking around wildlife is a bad test of moderate trainability. Plan the adult size, the vet, and the daily work before the puppy is on the way home.

Socialize a Finnish Spitz during the early weeks, roughly 3 to 14 weeks, when a barking bird dog is still deciding who counts as normal. Include strangers, because aloofness is part of the package, and include other dogs and children under control. Pair every new sound with something the puppy wants, or you will rehearse alarm barking at leaves. Do not socialize by letting the puppy chase squirrels. That prey drive is already strong. Premium food is $400 to $900 a year for this 20 to 33 pound body, and training treats should come out of meals so the bird dog does not get a second career as a counter thief.

Classes help a Finnish Spitz only if the room can tolerate a dog that talks. Use them for a recall that has a chance against prey, a settle, and a quiet cue, then keep taking the dog out so strangers stay boring. Manners class will not delete the bark. It can put the bark on a switch some of the time. Continue through adolescence. Hypothyroidism and patellar luxation are reasons to keep the dog at a lean working weight, and insurance at $350 to $700 is easier to buy before a knee or a thyroid panel is already on the invoice. Routine veterinary care is $300 to $600.

A day with a Finnish Spitz has a hunt-shaped outing, a brushing session in shedding season, and a plan for the bark when the mail comes. Moderate-to-high exercise can be sniffing, bird-dog games, and a fenced run, not a silent apartment treadmill. Chew toys matter because a 13 to 15 year companion with moderate trainability will invent work. Watch for a skip in the hind leg that could be patellar luxation, and for the weight gain or dull coat that can come with hypothyroidism. Supplies run $150 to $350. The dog should sleep in the house, not in a noise-clause flat.

Routine is useful, and it has to include the Finnish Spitz's own signals. A skipped breakfast, a quieter-than-usual voice, or a limp is data, not a scheduling error. Feed from the $400 to $900 food range on a clock so you notice. Keep the fence closed even when the recall looked perfect yesterday, because squirrels still win. If you wanted a quiet white spitz, this reddish barking bird dog will feel like a mistake by the end of the first week. Lifespan is 13 to 15 years when the knees, thyroid, hips, and epilepsy questions in the line are faced early rather than after a crisis.

The Flat-Coated Retriever was built as a dual-purpose gundog that could hunt all day and still greet you as if the day had just started. Adults are about 60 to 70 pounds and 22 to 24 inches, cheerful, optimistic, and good-humored, excellent with children, with moderate shedding and high needs for both exercise and grooming. The lifespan on this card is 8 to 10 years, shorter than many retrievers, so the cheerful years are concentrated. Food runs $600 to $1,200, grooming $300 to $600, and insurance $400 to $800. Buy the dog for the working temperament, and read that lifespan before you fall for the otter tail.

The Smooth Fox Terrier was developed to bolt foxes and dispatch vermin, and the 15 to 19 pound, 15 inch dog still has that bold, independent terrier mind. The modern companion is friendly and good with children, with high exercise, moderate shedding, and low grooming needs. Lifespan runs 12 to 15 years. A short smooth coat does not make this a lap breed. The original job was underground courage, and a bored adult will apply that courage to the garden, the cat next door, or the couch.

DNA tests are only as useful as the conditions someone in this Smooth Fox Terrier's line has actually named. This card does not list a signature genetic disease, so a glossy panel with no family history is not a clean bill of health. Ask which relatives lived into the 12 to 15 year span and which did not, and keep ordinary veterinary care at the listed $300 to $600. Bold and independent is a temperament fact, not a diagnosis. Spend screening money where the breeder can point to a reason.

Through the middle years, a Smooth Fox Terrier still wants high daily exercise on a 15 to 19 pound frame that looks tougher than it is. Keep jumping and hard landings thoughtful as the dog ages inside a 12 to 15 year life, and watch weight, because a short coat hides very little fat but owners still overfeed a friendly beggar. Low grooming needs, about $100 to $300 a year, mean you can see skin and teeth easily. Use that. A bold dog that skips a meal or softens on a walk is easier to spot than in a heavy-coated breed, if you are looking.

Budgets for a Smooth Fox Terrier split between a modest body and a busy brain. Premium food is $300 to $600, routine care $300 to $600, insurance $300 to $600, grooming only $100 to $300, first-year training $200 to $500, and supplies $150 to $300. Some owners land at the low end if the dog stays sound for 12 to 15 years. Others spend past the high end on teeth, injuries from high exercise, or a second round of training because an independent terrier ignored the first one. The table is a range, not a quote.

Early Smooth Fox Terrier spending is the fence, the $200 to $500 training start, and replacing whatever a vermin-hunter chews while you are still building a recall. Food at $300 to $600 does not look dramatic until you add supplies at $150 to $300 that disappear into a crate graveyard. After the first year the coat stays cheap to keep, at $100 to $300, and the cost that returns is veterinary care if an aging terrier inside a 12 to 15 year life slows down. Buy insurance, listed at $300 to $600, before that slowdown has a name.

Keeping a Smooth Fox Terrier on a schedule of exams beats hoping a bold dog will announce pain. The breed is friendly and independent, which can look like toughness right up to a dental crisis or a limp from high exercise. The routine veterinary line sits at $300 to $600. Use it. A short coat and low grooming bill do not include dentistry. Across 12 to 15 years, the dogs that stay easy to live with are the lean ones whose owners did not wait for an independent terrier to volunteer that something hurt.

Feed a Smooth Fox Terrier as a small, high-exercise terrier, 15 to 19 pounds, not as a generic white dog from a costume shop. Premium food at $300 to $600 covers a measured cup. A German Pinscher fits a home that can give an hour-plus of work, an experienced hand, and a fence against prey drive. Children go better when they are older. Screen a German Wirehaired Pointer like the versatile hunting dog it is. The Greater Swiss Mountain Dog was a Swiss farm draft dog, used to drive cattle and pull carts, and it is neither a sighthound nor a livestock guardian in the Kangal pattern. Living well with a Greater Swiss Mountain Dog means respecting 85 to 140 pounds of faithful draft dog that is excellent with children and still capable of leaning, drooling, and deciding the hallway is a cart path. Social life for a Greater Swiss Mountain Dog is family-first. Puppies that are handled by children, guests, and the veterinarian grow into the family-oriented temperament the card describes. Household energy for a Greater Swiss Mountain Dog is moderate exercise plus a brain that was bred to work a farm, not two hours of fetch on pavement. Keep a Greater Swiss Mountain Dog lean and looked at, because 8 to 11 years is not a long time to waste on extra weight. Routine veterinary care is $300 to $600. Spend the Greater Swiss Mountain Dog's preventive budget on weight checks, joint-friendly exercise, and a yearly hands-on exam of a dog that can hide discomfort under a dependable temperament. A Greater Swiss Mountain Dog label should show a complete-and-balanced statement and a calorie number you can turn into a daily portion for a 23 to 28 inch dog. A Greyhound is a sighthound, a sprinter that lives as a quiet house dog, and it is a bad description to call one a flock guardian. Greyhound screening is practical rather than fashionable. Ask whether a retired racer was tested for Babesia and Ehrlichia. A Harrier is a pack scent hound, smaller than an American Foxhound, and it is not a sighthound and not a flock guardian. The first Harrier year pays for high exercise gear, a second dog or a serious dog-sport plan if you do not already have a pack, and training at $200 to $500 aimed at a recall that loses to a scent. Spend time around Harriers before you commit, because the friendly greeting comes with a bay, a pack preference, and selective attention on a scent. An Ibizan Hound ages inside an 11 to 14 year span as a sighthound that is clownish outside and quiet on the couch, not as a flock guardian that patrols stock. Pick Irish Doodle food for the dog you have, somewhere between 40 and 70 pounds, with high exercise and a coat that may be low-shed and still need moderate grooming at $100 to $300. The Irish Red and White Setter is a pointing gundog, lighter than many people expect at 35 to 60 pounds and 22 to 26 inches, courageous, spirited, and friendly. Social learning for an Irish Red and White Setter runs from a mouthy, friendly puppy to a spirited adult that still wants to greet the world at a hunting pace. An Irish Red and White Setter often stays playful deep into an 11 to 15 year life, then gives you a shorter point and a longer nap. Friendly does not become suspicious with age in a well-kept setter. Pain can look like a mood change. Food remains in the $600 to $1,200 band only if portions shrink with the mileage. A 35 to 60 pound dog gains easily once the hunting day shrinks.

Routine care for an Irish Red and White Setter is the unglamorous loop of ears, nails, waist, and a yearly exam inside $300 to $600, with insurance at $400 to $800 if a field injury or a late-life problem leaves that band. Judge an Irish Red and White Setter diet across the 11 to 15 year span, not across a week. Premium food is $600 to $1,200 for a 22 to 26 inch dog doing high exercise. On the bag for this setter, look for a named meat as the first ingredient, an AAFCO statement that the food is complete for the life stage, and a calorie-per-cup figure you can portion against 35 to 60 pounds of high exercise.
